Elementary proof that, in a topos, every epimorphism is regular?

Ask Question
Asked 3 months ago
Modified 3 months ago
Viewed 146 times
This question shows research effort; it is useful and clear
6
Save this question.
Show activity on this post.

Mac Lane and Moerdijk have a neat proof on p. 197 that, in a topos EE, every epimorphism f:C→Bf:C→B is a coequalizer. But this depends on the assumption that the slice category E/BE/B is itself a topos.

The Elephant gets there sooner, and has a proof by p. 38 that, in a (pre)topos, every epimorphism is a coequalizer. But again this depends on some moderately fancy earlier moves.

So here's the question: is there a significantly more elementary proof of the result which requires less scene-setting, requires only relatively small steps on from the definition of an elementary topos?

I had the impression that I'd somewhere, sometime, seen a simpler proof (indeed, maybe even here on math.se??). But I can't locate one: so maybe I'm just having a senior moment!

  • The two arguments are actually the same. a) If a category has a subobject classifier, then all monomorphisms are strong. b) If all monomorphisms are strong, then all epimorphisms are strong. c) If coequalizers of kernel pairs exist and have pullbacks that are epimorphisms, then every morphism factors as a regular epimorphism followed by a monomorphism. d) A strong monomorphism factors as a regular epimorphism followed by a monomorphism if and only if it is regular. The two hypotheses for c) hold in a topos by monadicity of contravariant power object functor and local cartesian closure.
    – Vladimir Sotirov
    Commented Mar 17 at 22:38
  • This question then amounts to whether one can show strong epis are regular in a topos without showing that coequalizers of kernel pairs both exist and have pullbacks that are epimorphisms.
    – Vladimir Sotirov
    Commented Mar 17 at 22:41

  • I think I have an argument which is fairly elementary, except that it uses the fact that any morphism in a topos which is a monomorphism and an epimorphism is an isomorphism. Would that count as elementary enough? (I don't remember exactly how that latter fact is bootstrapped in a topos.)
    – Daniel Schepler

We will show that in fact, any epimorphism f:C→Bf:C→B in a topos is effective, i.e. ff is the coequalizer of the two projections C×BC→CC×BC→C. Thus, suppose we have a morphism g:C→Xg:C→X such that g∘π1=g∘π2g∘π1=g∘π2. Then set II to be the image of (f,g):C→B×X(f,g):C→B×X. We claim that the first projection I→BI→B is an isomorphism; then the required morphism B→XB→X will be the composition of the inverse of I→BI→B with the second projection I→XI→X (and the uniqueness of the map B→XB→X will be an immediate consequence of ff being an epimorphism).

To see this, first note that the projection π¯1:I→Bπ¯1:I→B is certainly an epimorphism, since π1∘(f,g)=fπ1∘(f,g)=f is an epimorphism. Therefore, we reduce to showing that the projection I→BI→B is a monomorphism. To see this, suppose we have two morphisms i,j:U→Ii,j:U→I such that π¯1∘i=π¯1∘jπ¯1∘i=π¯1∘j. Then there exists an epimorphism V→UV→U and two morphisms i¯,j¯:V→Ci¯,j¯:V→C making appropriate commutative diagrams with i,ji,j respectively. But then the fact that π¯1∘i=π¯1∘jπ¯1∘i=π¯1∘j implies that (i¯,j¯)(i¯,j¯) induces a morphism V→C×BCV→C×BC. Therefore, the assumption g∘π1=g∘π2g∘π1=g∘π2 implies that g∘i¯=g∘j¯g∘i¯=g∘j¯; and from V→UV→U being an epimorphism, we get that π¯2∘i=π¯2∘jπ¯2∘i=π¯2∘j also. From here, we can conclude that in fact i=ji=j.

In case there is any difficulty in filling in the details of this argument, let me just comment that this is a categorization of this completely elementary argument for the case of SetSet: first, with the given setup, the assumption g∘π1=g∘π2g∘π1=g∘π2 amounts to the requirement that whenever c1,c2:Cc1,c2:C are such that f(c1)=f(c2)f(c1)=f(c2), then g(c1)=g(c2)g(c1)=g(c2). Now, I={(b,x):B×X∣∃c:C,f(c)=b∧g(c)=x}I={(b,x):B×X∣∃c:C,f(c)=b∧g(c)=x}. It is immediate from ff being surjective that every b:Bb:B occurs as a first coordinate of an element of II. On the other hand, if (b,x1),(b,x2)∈I(b,x1),(b,x2)∈I, then there exist c1,c2:Cc1,c2:C such that f(c1)=f(c2)=bf(c1)=f(c2)=b, g(c1)=x1g(c1)=x1, and g(c2)=x2g(c2)=x2. But then the assumption g∘π1=g∘π2g∘π1=g∘π2 gives x1=x2x1=x2. Thus, we have shown that II is the graph of some function B→XB→X.

(Also, let me observe that the dependencies of the topos case argument are: that a topos is balanced, i.e. every morphism which is a monomorphism and an epimorphism is an isomorphism; the existence of images, i.e. epi-mono factorizations; and that in a topos, epimorphisms are stable under pullbacks.)
